projects.title: How a Solar Panel Turns Sunlight Into Electricity
projects.prompt: Solar panel. Photons. Silicon. Electrons. Holes. Electric field. Direct current. Inverter.

lines.text: A solar panel turns sunlight directly into electricity for your home.
The working part is not the glass cover; it is the thin solar cell underneath.
When sunlight enters the solar cell, photons transfer energy to electrons in the silicon.
That energy frees some electrons, leaving behind positively charged vacancies called holes.
A built-in electric field inside the solar cell pushes the freed electrons in one direction.
Metal contacts collect those electrons and send their flow through an external circuit as direct current.
The moving electrons can power a load before returning to the solar cell.
For many home appliances, an inverter changes the solar panel's direct current into alternating current.
So the solar panel supplies electricity because sunlight frees charges and the cell guides their flow.

scenes: Direct current flows through a load

projects.title: How a Heat Pump Warms Your Home
projects.prompt: Heat pump. Refrigerant. Outdoor coil. Evaporation. Compressor. Indoor coil. Expansion valve.

lines.text: A heat pump warms your home by moving heat from outdoor air, even when that air feels cold.
It transports existing heat rather than creating heat from nothing.
Outside, cold refrigerant absorbs heat from the air and evaporates into a gas.
The heat pump's compressor squeezes this gas, raising its pressure and temperature.
The hot gas enters the indoor coil and releases its heat into your home.
A fan blows across that coil, carrying the released heat into your rooms.
The refrigerant condenses into a liquid as it gives up heat.
An expansion valve then lowers its pressure, making it cold again for the outdoor coil.
This repeating refrigeration cycle is how the heat pump moves heat indoors.

scenes: A heat pump moves existing heat
The indoor coil heats your rooms
The refrigerant resets for another cycle

projects.title: How an Accelerometer Counts Your Steps
projects.prompt: Accelerometer. Proof mass. Springs. Capacitor fingers. Acceleration. Filter. Step counter.

lines.text: Your phone or fitness band can count steps with a tiny chip called an accelerometer.
Inside this accelerometer, a microscopic proof mass shifts slightly when your body moves.
Tiny flexible springs hold the mass inside the chip while allowing that small movement.
As the mass shifts, the spacing between interlocking capacitor fingers changes.
The accelerometer's electronics convert that spacing change into an acceleration signal.
During walking, the signal contains a repeating pattern from each step and other body motion.
Software filters noise and looks for the rhythm and strength of genuine steps, rather than counting every bump.
Each accepted step pattern advances the step counter by one.
So your step count begins with motion inside the accelerometer and ends with software recognizing a walking pattern.

scenes: A tiny sensor inside your device
The proof mass responds to motion
From microscopic motion to a step count

projects.title: How a 3D Printer Builds an Object
projects.prompt: 3D printer. Slicer. Layers. Toolpath. Nozzle. Filament. Extrusion. Cooling. Layer bonding.

lines.text: A 3D printer builds a solid object by depositing material one thin layer at a time.
First, slicing software divides a digital 3D model into a stack of printable layers.
For each layer, the slicer calculates the nozzle's path around the outer walls and through the inner structure.
The printer heats the nozzle until the plastic filament can flow through its tip.
Motors drive the nozzle along the calculated path while it extrudes a thin bead of melted plastic.
The deposited plastic cools and solidifies, forming the current layer of your object.
The nozzle then rises by one layer height, or the bed lowers, and the printer repeats the process.
Each new layer fuses with the previous one, gradually building a solid shape.
So a 3D printer turns a digital model into an object through repeated extrusion, cooling, and layer bonding.

scenes: An object built from thin layers
The printer deposits and cools a layer
From digital model to solid object

projects.title: How an Airbag Protects You in a Crash
projects.prompt: Airbag. Seat belt. Crash sensor. Deceleration. Control unit. Igniter. Gas generator. Cushion. Vents.

lines.text: In a severe car crash, an airbag works with your seat belt to cushion you from hard interior surfaces.
This explanation slows the sequence down; in a real crash, the airbag responds in tens of milliseconds.
Crash sensors detect the vehicle's sudden deceleration and send that information to the airbag control unit.
The control unit triggers the airbag only when the crash pattern indicates a severe impact.
A small igniter then activates a gas generator inside the folded airbag module.
The generator rapidly produces gas that flows into the woven fabric cushion.
The expanding airbag spreads out in front of the occupant, distributing force over a wider area.
As you press into the cushion, vents let gas escape so the airbag can absorb motion while deflating.
So the airbag protects by sensing a crash, inflating quickly, and then yielding in a controlled way.

scenes: Sensors and the control unit detect a severe crash
The cushion spreads force and deflates
